newsitem.title: USA: Cohen to call for more U.S. base closures.
newsitem.headline: Cohen to call for more U.S. base closures.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Cohen will press Congress to close more domestic military bases and approve up to $2 billion in extra funds for missile defence in a major defence strategy report this month, the Pentagon said on Tuesday.

"He will seek additional base closures," Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters following warnings from Cohen that more base closures were needed to catch up with U.S. troop cuts made since the end of the Cold War.

Other defence officials told Reuters privately that Cohen will seek two new rounds of politically painful base closings in 1999 and 2001 and would propose a minimal cut of 60,000 troops in the 1.4 million-member U.S. armed forces.

Defence officials confirmed a Washington Post report that Cohen had decided to recommend some reduction in numbers in planned jet fighter programmes for the Air Force and Navy, but gave no details of the cuts.
The newspaper also said Cohen would propose shrinking the Navy's fleet.

The moves are all part of the so-called quadrennial defence review (QDR), which is aimed at preserving a superpower military with more modern weapons in the face of static defence budgets in the years to come.
The Defence Department has already shut or is closing dozens of big domestic bases and hundreds of smaller facilities in four rounds of domestic closings that are scheduled to be completed in 2001.
Cohen himself said in a speech to business executives in Washington on Tuesday night on the QDR: "We should ask Congress ... should we protect facilities instead of protecting our forces?"

He declined to give details of the report, which is scheduled to go to Congress on May 15, but added that he would name a team of experts on Friday to study additional cuts in the bureaucracy of his own office in order to save money for weapons modernisation.
"Let me tell you, in my judgment the office of secretary of defence is too big, is too bureaucratic and it has to be reformed," he said.

Cohen said that the panel would recommend by year's end cuts in the office of the secretary, which controls much of the vast civilian bureaucracy at the Pentagon. Defence officials said the group would be headed by Arnold Punaro, former chief of staff of the Senate Intelligence Committee.

Department spokesman Bacon told reporters earlier on Tuesday that the QDR would also seek between $1 billion and $2 billion in additional funding to develop a possible national defence against missile attack.

Bacon declined to give details of the new base closings plan, but other defence officials said privately that Cohen intended to press lawmakers to approve an additional two rounds of closings, one beginning in 1999 and the other in 2001.
Such moves are economically devastating for many communities, which depend on military payrolls and purchasing power.

Cohen noted in recent speeches that the U.S. armed forces has slashed troop strength by one-third to 1.4 million since the Soviet Union collapsed, but only 18 percent of basing structure has been cut at home and abroad.
Hundreds of big and small U.S. military facilities have also been closed overseas in recent years. The secretary can order the closure of overseas bases without approval from Congress.

Congress earlier passed laws that allowed for the four rounds of domestic closings overseen by base closing and realignment commissions (BRAC). The independent commissions would draw up closing lists that would have to be either approved or rejected as a whole by Congress.

On the missile defence issue, the Washington Times reported on Tuesday that the Pentagon was behind budget and schedule on a plan to develop technologies and weapons for a possible national missile defence by 1999.

Bacon said the QDR would recommend additional spending of between $1 billion and $2 billion to prepare technology for a potential national missile defence by 1999 in case the Pentagon decided then that such a system should be deployed by the year 2003.

The Clinton administration has rejected pressure from Congressional Republicans to revive former President Ronald Reagan's dream of a so-called "Star Wars" anti-missile umbrella over the United States, opting instead for a less-ambitious programme to protect troops and bases.
But the Pentagon has agreed to work on technologies for a national missile defence and to have them ready for a decision by 1999 to deploy later if the need arises.
